newsitem.title: USA: Aluminum demand seen outpacing supply - Spector.
newsitem.headline: Aluminum demand seen outpacing supply - Spector.

text.p: World aluminum demand is expected to outpace supply over the next five years, aided by the increased use of aluminum automotive applications, industry expert Stewart Spector said.
Spector, publisher of the Spector Report, an aluminum industry service, spoke before a conference entitled "The Aluminum Scrap Gap" sponsored by industry consultants Gorham/Intertech Consulting.
"Despite what may appear to be an abundant supply of aluminium at the moment, from 1997 to at least the year 2000, the growth in demand for primary ingot could be supply constrained," Spector said.

Since 1970, the world automotive industry has been using more alumimum in cars and light trucks. "Over the next ten years automotive use could double and rise by another 50 percent by the year 2010," Spector said.
The world average net weight content of aluminum per passenger car is estimated to be 225 lbs in 1996 up from 140 lbs in 1990 and 64 lbs in 1970.
"By 1998, it could reach 275 lbs per car and 375 lbs by 2000 and possibly in the range of 375-600 lbs by 2005 to 2010," Spector said.
Also, Asia, Latin America and Eastern Europe are turning to primary ingot for their needs as these economies grow.
"The emerging economies of the world in 1995 and 1996 consume approximately 6.4 million tonnes of primary aluminum or one third of total western world shipments," he said.
In four years, Spector expects the emerging economies to consume an additional 2.3 million tonnes to about 8.7 million tonnes versus the 6.4 million tonnes consumed in 1996.
He noted ingot from the Commonwealth of Independent States, which had been a supply problem for the West, could become less available as Eastern Europe economies recover.
Spector added that the industry needs about 1.9 months inventory-to-sales ratio.
By the end of 1996, he sees the ratio to be about 2.1 months or about 267,000 tonnes above the desired level of 1.9 months.

"Next year, if western world shipments rise by 5.5 to 6.0 percent as forecast, stocks would drop by 400,000 tonnes-plus and the inventory-to-sales ratio falls to 1.7 months, which now becomes a deficit," he said.
Spector, anticipating a scrap gap, expects the initial supply source of automotive use to be primary aluminum by the year 2000.
"Now 60 to 70 percent of aluminum used in automobiles is comprised of secondary metallics. This will change," he said.

Aluminum scrap now coming back from scrapped cars is already being recycled back into the aluminum supply chain in one form or another. "The only other source of alumimum supply is primary ingot," he said.

"Thus, in a theoretical sense, depending upon auto scrappage rates, the automotive use of primary aluminum could account for most of the incremental growth in demand for primary ingot by the year 2000 and beyond," Spector said.
